# Introduction
Terrestrial ecosystems play an important role in regulating exchanges of carbon, water and energy between the land surface and the atmosphere. Ecosystem productivity and carbon fluxes are influenced by environmental conditions, including temperature, water availability, soil properties, vegetation characteristics and extreme climatic events.

Eddy covariance measurements provide valuable information on ecosystem–atmosphere exchanges. Standardized FLUXNET data products facilitate comparisons of carbon, water and energy fluxes across ecosystems [@pastorello2020]. However, integrating these measurements with complementary environmental datasets can improve our understanding of the factors associated with spatial and temporal variability in ecosystem functioning.

This report investigates the relationships between environmental conditions and ecosystem productivity across five FLUXNET sites representing contrasting ecosystem types: deciduous broadleaf forest, evergreen needleleaf forest, grassland, cropland and wetland. FLUXNET observations are integrated with complementary environmental datasets to explore site-specific responses to environmental variability and identify potential differences in the factors associated with ecosystem productivity and carbon fluxes.

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(stringr)
library(purrr)
library(lubridate)
library(knitr)
library(patchwork)
```

```{r}
# ecosystem color palette
eco_cols <- c(
  "DBF" = "#2E7D32",  # dark green
  "ENF" = "#2A9D8F",  # teal green
  "GRA" = "#90BE6D",  # light green
  "CRO" = "#E9C46A",  # mustard yellow
  "WET" = "#8ECAE6"   # light blue
)

# site metadata
sites_tbl <- tibble(
  site_id = c("JP-Api", "CA-Ca1", "CH-Rtb", "CZ-KrP", "US-Elm"),
  igbp = c("DBF", "ENF", "GRA", "CRO", "WET"),
  site_name = c(
    "Appi forest meteorology research site",
    "British Columbia - 1949 Douglas-fir stand",
    "Rietholzbach",
    "Kresin u Pacova",
    "Everglades (long hydroperiod marsh)"
  ),
  country = c("Japan", "Canada", "Switzerland", "Czechia", "USA")

```

```{r}
#| label: load-merged-data
#| include: false

data_dir <- if (dir.exists("data/processed")) {
  "data/processed"
} else {
  "../data/processed"
}

site_static <- read_csv(
  file.path(data_dir, "site_static.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

site_daily <- read_csv(
  file.path(data_dir, "site_daily.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

site_daily <- site_daily |>
  mutate(
    date = as.Date(date),
    year = year(date),
    month = month(date)
  )

# Add ecosystem classification
if (!"igbp" %in% names(site_daily)) {
  site_daily <- site_daily |>
    left_join(
      site_static |> select(site_id, igbp),
      by = "site_id"
    )
}
```

# Materials and methods

The five selected FLUXNET sites differ in ecosystem type, geographical location and temporal coverage. As shown in the Block 4 summary, all sites exhibit incomplete measurement coverage, and the proportion of directly measured flux observations varies among sites and years. Therefore, the flux datasets should be interpreted as partially gap-filled observational products rather than continuous complete measurements. These differences in data availability are important to consider when comparing patterns among sites.

## Study sites

The study comprises five eddy covariance stations distributed across  Asia, Europe and North America, representing contrasting ecosystem  types and climatic conditions. All sites are located in the Northern  Hemisphere, with four sites in temperate or cool-temperate regions  and one in a subtropical region. Differences in vegetation  characteristics, hydrological conditions, land use and temporal  coverage provide a basis for exploring site-specific relationships between environmental drivers and ecosystem functioning.

The selected stations include the Appi deciduous broadleaf forest (JP-Api; DBF) in Japan [@yasuda2026], the Douglas-fir evergreen  needleleaf forest (CA-Ca1; ENF) in British Columbia, Canada  [@black2025], the Rietholzbach grassland (CH-Rtb; GRA) in  Switzerland [@hirschi2026], the Kresin u Pacova cropland  (CZ-KrP; CRO) in Czechia [@acosta2026], and the Everglades  long-hydroperiod permanent wetland (US-Elm; WET) in southern  Florida, United States [@starr2026].

Ecosystem types are described according to the International  Geosphere–Biosphere Programme (IGBP) land-cover classification.  The geographical characteristics and monitoring periods of the  five stations are summarized in @tbl-study-sites, and their spatial distribution is illustrated in @fig-study-sites.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-study-sites
#| tbl-cap: "Geographical characteristics, ecosystem classifications and monitoring periods of the five FLUXNET study sites."

site_static |>
  mutate(
    ecosystem = recode(
      igbp,
      "DBF" = "Deciduous broadleaf forest",
      "ENF" = "Evergreen needleleaf forest",
      "GRA" = "Grassland",
      "CRO" = "Cropland",
      "WET" = "Permanent wetland"
    ),
    country_name = recode(
      country,
      "JP" = "Japan",
      "CA" = "Canada",
      "CH" = "Switzerland",
      "CZ" = "Czechia",
      "US" = "USA"
    ),
    period = paste(first_year, last_year, sep = "–")
  ) |>
  select(
    site_id,
    country_name,
    igbp,
    ecosystem,
    lat,
    lon,
    period
  ) |>
  rename(
    "Site" = site_id,
    "Country" = country_name,
    "IGBP" = igbp,
    "Ecosystem type" = ecosystem,
    "Latitude (°)" = lat,
    "Longitude (°)" = lon,
    "Monitoring period" = period
  ) |>
  kable(digits = 2)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-study-sites
#| fig-cap: "Geographical distribution of the five FLUXNET study sites. Colors indicate ecosystem classifications."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5

world <- map_data("world")

ggplot() +
  geom_polygon(
    data = world,
    aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group),
    fill = "#E8E6DF",
    color = "white",
    linewidth = 0.15
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = site_static,
    aes(x = lon, y = lat, fill = igbp),
    shape = 21,
    color = "grey30",
    size = 4
  ) +
  geom_text(
    data = site_static,
    aes(x = lon, y = lat, label = site_id),
    nudge_y = 5,
    check_overlap = TRUE,
    size = 3
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = eco_cols) +
  coord_quickmap(
    xlim = c(-180, 180),
    ylim = c(-60, 85)
  ) +
  labs(fill = "Ecosystem") +
  theme_void() +
  theme(
    panel.background = element_rect(
      fill = "#E7F2F6",
      color = NA
    ),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )
```

## FLUXNET data and data coverage

Daily FLUXNET observations from the five study sites investigated in Block 4 were used as the basis for this analysis. The datasets include carbon fluxes and meteorological variables processed using standardized FLUXNET procedures (Pastorello et al., 2020).

The preliminary assessment conducted in Block 4 revealed substantial differences in measurement coverage among sites and years. Based on half-hourly NEE quality flags, the proportion of records classified as gap-filled ranged from 31.0% at US-Elm to 68.0% at CA-Ca1. These proportions describe NEE quality flags and do not directly represent the quality or gap-filled fractions of GPP and ecosystem respiration estimates.

No additional gap-filling was performed in the present analysis. Missing observations were retained as missing values and excluded from individual analyses when the required variables were unavailable. The number of valid observations was reported for each analysis where appropriate.

## Complementary environmental datasets

Eight complementary environmental datasets were selected to  characterize the climatic, edaphic and biological conditions  of the five FLUXNET study sites. The datasets differ in spatial  resolution, temporal coverage and methodological approach  (@tbl-provenance). These differences were considered during  data integration and interpretation of the results.

| Dataset | Spatial resolution | Temporal coverage | Data source | Reference |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ERA5-Land | 0.1° (~9 km) | Hourly, 1950–present | [Copernicus CDS](https://cds.climate.copernicus.eu/) | [@munoz2021] |
| WorldClim 2.1 | 5 arc-min (~9 km at equator) | 1970–2000 normals | [WorldClim](https://worldclim.org/) | [@fick2017] |
| Dheed | 0.25° | Daily, 1950–2023 | [Zenodo](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.14884254) | [@weynants2025] |
| SoilGrids 2.0 | 250 m | Static | [ISRIC](https://soilgrids.org/) | [@poggio2021] |
| PlantTraits | 1 km | Static | [Zenodo](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.14646322) | [@lusk2026] |
| deadtrees.earth | 10 m | Annual | [deadtrees.earth](https://deadtrees.earth/) | [@mosig2026] |
| iNaturalist | Georeferenced observations | Variable | [iNaturalist](https://www.inaturalist.org/) | [@inaturalist2026] |
| MODIS MOD13Q1 | 250 m | 16-day composites | [NASA LP DAAC](https://doi.org/10.5067/MODIS/MOD13Q1.061) | [@didan2021] |

: Provenance and spatiotemporal characteristics of the complementary environmental datasets selected for this study. {#tbl-provenance}

### ERA5-Land

ERA5-Land is a global land surface reanalysis dataset providing hourly environmental variables at a spatial resolution of approximately 9 km [@munoz2021]. Air temperature, soil temperature and volumetric soil water content at three soil depths (0–7, 7–28 and 28–100 cm) were obtained through the Copernicus Climate Data Store (CDS). Data were extracted for the grid cell nearest to each tower, covering up to the final ten years of its FLUXNET monitoring period. Hourly observations were aggregated into daily means.

### WorldClim

WorldClim 2.1 provides spatially interpolated climatic variables derived from meteorological station records [@fick2017]. Long-term climate normals for the period 1970–2000 were extracted at a spatial resolution of 5 arc-minutes (approximately 9 km at the equator). Mean annual temperature (BIO1), annual precipitation (BIO12), temperature seasonality (BIO4) and precipitation seasonality (BIO15) were used to characterize the climatic conditions of the study sites and provide a reference for assessing annual climatic anomalies.

### Dheed

Compound dry-hot extreme events were identified using Dheed, an ERA5-based global database covering the period 1950–2023 [@weynants2025]. The dataset provides daily information at a spatial resolution of 0.25° and identifies compound extreme events through the spatial and temporal connectivity of simultaneously dry and hot conditions.

Daily event labels were extracted for the grid cell corresponding to each FLUXNET tower and integrated with daily carbon flux records using the site identifier and date. The analysis was restricted to the overlapping temporal coverage of both datasets. Consequently, FLUXNET observations from 2024 at US-Elm were excluded from the Dheed analysis.

### SoilGrids

Soil physicochemical properties were obtained from SoilGrids 2.0 [@poggio2021], a global spatial dataset providing predictions of soil characteristics at approximately 250 m resolution. SoilGrids estimates include soil texture, organic carbon and other soil properties at different depths. The extracted values were linked to the five FLUXNET sites using their geographical coordinates.

Because SoilGrids provides model-based predictions rather than direct measurements at the flux towers, these values were treated as estimates of local soil conditions. Missing values were retained as missing, and no additional gap-filling or imputation was performed.

### PlantTraits

Spatially mapped plant functional traits were obtained from the PlantTraits dataset [@lusk2026]. The selected characteristics include specific leaf area (SLA), leaf nitrogen content, rooting depth, leaf area, stem density and plant height. Prediction uncertainty and the area of applicability were considered when interpreting these estimates, particularly for cropland and wetland ecosystems, where the model may have limited applicability.

### deadtrees.earth

Spatial information on tree cover and standing deadwood was obtained from deadtrees.earth [@mosig2026]. The geographical coverage and applicability of the dataset were assessed for the five study sites. Particular attention was given to the interpretation of tree cover and standing deadwood around non-forest ecosystems, such as the grassland CH-Rtb and cropland CZ-KrP.

### iNaturalist

Georeferenced species observation records were obtained from iNaturalist [@inaturalist2026] within the surroundings of each FLUXNET tower. The records were used to characterize documented species occurrences and explore potential relationships between seasonal biological observations and ecosystem productivity. Differences in observation effort, accessibility and reporting activity were considered when comparing species records among sites.

### MODIS

Satellite-derived vegetation information was obtained from the MODIS Terra MOD13Q1 Version 6.1 product, which provides 16-day vegetation index composites at a spatial resolution of 250 m [@didan2021]. The normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI) and enhanced vegetation index (EVI) were calculated from spectral reflectance data and compared with the corresponding official MODIS vegetation indices. These variables were integrated with FLUXNET GPP observations to investigate seasonal relationships between vegetation greenness and ecosystem productivity.


## Data preparation and integration
FLUXNET observations and complementary environmental datasets were integrated using the provided `09_merge.R` script. Two primary tables were generated: a static table containing site-level environmental characteristics and a daily table containing FLUXNET observations and available time-varying environmental variables. Static variables were associated with each tower using the site identifier (`site_id`), while daily observations were matched using the site identifier and date.

Annual datasets, including standing deadwood cover, were considered separately at their corresponding temporal resolution. FLUXNET daily observations are recorded in local standard time, whereas ERA5-Land daily values are aggregated in UTC. This temporal difference was considered when interpreting daily relationships.

```{r}
#| label: daily-data-coverage

daily_coverage <- site_daily |>
  group_by(site_id) |>
  summarise(
    across(
      everything(),
      ~ round(mean(!is.na(.x)) * 100, 1)
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

daily_coverage
```

## Statistical and graphical analyses
Exploratory analyses were designed to investigate relationships between environmental variables and ecosystem productivity at each study site. Time series, scatterplots, descriptive statistics and correlation analyses were used where appropriate. Analyses were conducted at temporal resolutions consistent with the characteristics of the corresponding datasets.

Site-specific relationships were examined separately to account for differences in ecosystem type, climatic conditions and measurement periods. Comparisons involving static environmental characteristics were interpreted descriptively because only five independent study sites were available.

# Results

## Site environmental portrait

The environmental characteristics of the five study sites were compared using long-term climatic normals from WorldClim, estimated plant functional traits from PlantTraits and species observation records from iNaturalist. Table 2 summarizes the climatic conditions, vegetation characteristics and recorded biodiversity surrounding each tower.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-environmental-portrait
#| tbl-cap: "Climatic, plant functional and biodiversity characteristics of the five FLUXNET study sites."

site_static |>
  select(
    site_id,
    igbp,
    BIO1,
    BIO12,
    SLA,
    leaf_N_mass,
    rooting_depth,
    n_species
  ) |>
  rename(
    "Site ID" = site_id,
    "Ecosystem" = igbp,
    "Mean annual temperature (°C)" = BIO1,
    "Annual precipitation (mm)" = BIO12,
    "Specific leaf area (m²/kg)" = SLA,
    "Leaf nitrogen (mg/g)" = leaf_N_mass,
    "Rooting depth (m)" = rooting_depth,
    "Recorded species" = n_species
  ) |>
  kable(digits = 2)
```

The four temperate and cool-temperate sites exhibited similar mean annual temperatures, ranging from 7.14 to 7.64 °C, whereas the subtropical wetland US-Elm was considerably warmer (24.15 °C). Annual precipitation varied substantially among sites, with the highest value recorded at CA-Ca1 (1691 mm) and the lowest at CZ-KrP (585 mm).

Estimated specific leaf area and leaf nitrogen content were highest at the cropland site CZ-KrP and lowest at the wetland site US-Elm. The latter also exhibited the greatest estimated rooting depth (0.64 m). However, these trait estimates require further consideration of the model's area of applicability.

The highest numbers of species recorded through iNaturalist were observed at CH-Rtb (280 species) and US-Elm (269 species), while CZ-KrP had the lowest number of recorded species (34).

## ERA5-Land: Soil water and temperature

### Validation of ERA5-Land air temperature

To assess the agreement between ERA5-Land reanalysis data and FLUXNET air temperature records, daily air temperatures from both datasets were compared for each study site. The most recent year with at least 300 paired daily observations was selected independently for each tower. Agreement between the datasets was evaluated using Pearson's correlation coefficient, mean bias and root mean square error (RMSE).

```{r}
#| label: fig-era5-temperature-validation
#| fig-cap: "Daily air temperature from FLUXNET and ERA5-Land for the latest year with at least 300 paired observations at each site."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 8

temperature_check <- site_daily |>
  filter(
    !is.na(TA_F),
    !is.na(era5l_t2m_C)
  ) |>
  group_by(site_id, year) |>
  filter(n() >= 300) |>
  ungroup() |>
  group_by(site_id) |>
  filter(year == max(year)) |>
  ungroup()

temperature_long <- temperature_check |>
  select(
    site_id, igbp, year, date,
    TA_F, era5l_t2m_C
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(TA_F, era5l_t2m_C),
    names_to = "source",
    values_to = "temperature"
  )

ggplot(
  temperature_long,
  aes(
    x = date,
    y = temperature,
    color = igbp,
    linetype = source
  )
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~ site_id + year,
    scales = "free_x",
    ncol = 2
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(values = eco_cols) +
  scale_linetype_manual(
    values = c(
      "TA_F" = "solid",
      "era5l_t2m_C" = "dashed"
    ),
    labels = c(
      "TA_F" = "FLUXNET",
      "era5l_t2m_C" = "ERA5-Land"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Date",
    y = "Daily air temperature (°C)",
    color = "Ecosystem",
    linetype = "Data source"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-temperature-agreement
#| tbl-cap: "Agreement between daily FLUXNET and ERA5-Land air temperatures."

temperature_stats <- temperature_check |>
  group_by(site_id, igbp, year) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    correlation = cor(TA_F, era5l_t2m_C),
    bias = mean(era5l_t2m_C - TA_F),
    RMSE = sqrt(mean(
      (era5l_t2m_C - TA_F)^2
    )),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

temperature_stats |>
  rename(
    "Site ID" = site_id,
    "Ecosystem" = igbp,
    "Year" = year,
    "Paired days (n)" = n,
    "Pearson's r" = correlation,
    "Mean bias (°C)" = bias,
    "RMSE (°C)" = RMSE
  ) |>
  kable(digits = 2)
```

Daily air temperatures from ERA5-Land and FLUXNET exhibited strong positive correlations across all five study sites, with Pearson's correlation coefficients ranging from 0.91 to approximately 1.00 (Table 3). Both datasets captured the seasonal temperature patterns at each site (Figure 1).

The strongest agreement was observed at CZ-KrP, with an RMSE of 0.72 °C and a mean bias of 0.18 °C. Relatively close agreement was also observed at US-Elm, JP-Api and CH-Rtb, where RMSE values ranged from 1.38 to 1.90 °C.

In contrast, CA-Ca1 exhibited substantially larger temperature discrepancies, with an RMSE of 6.00 °C and a negative mean bias of −4.99 °C. Despite a strong positive correlation (r = 0.91), ERA5-Land systematically underestimated air temperatures at this site. Overall, the comparison comprised 1,826 paired daily observations across the five sites.

### Soil water limitation of productivity

**Research question:** Is there a soil moisture threshold below which summer GPP declines?

To investigate potential soil water limitations on ecosystem productivity, daily gross primary productivity (GPP) from FLUXNET was compared with volumetric soil water content at a depth of 7–28 cm obtained from ERA5-Land. The analysis was restricted to the Northern Hemisphere summer months (June–August). Only paired observations with available values for both variables were included. Site-specific scatterplots and locally weighted regression curves were used to explore potential nonlinear relationships and identify apparent soil moisture thresholds.

```{r}
#| label: fig-soil-water-gpp
#| fig-cap: "Relationship between daily volumetric soil water content at 7–28 cm depth and gross primary productivity during June–August across the five study sites."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 8

summer_data <- site_daily |>
  filter(
    month %in% c(6, 7, 8),
    !is.na(era5l_swvl2),
    !is.na(GPP_NT_VUT_REF)
  )

ggplot(
  summer_data,
  aes(
    x = era5l_swvl2,
    y = GPP_NT_VUT_REF,
    color = igbp
  )
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3, size = 0.8) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "loess",
    se = FALSE,
    linewidth = 1.2
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ site_id, ncol = 2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = eco_cols) +
  labs(
    x = "Volumetric soil water content (m³/m³)",
    y = "Daily GPP (g C/m²/day)",
    color = "Ecosystem"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-soil-water-gpp
#| tbl-cap: "Descriptive statistics for summer soil water content and gross primary productivity."

soil_stats <- summer_data |>
  group_by(site_id, igbp) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    n_years = n_distinct(year),
    mean_sm = mean(era5l_swvl2),
    min_sm = min(era5l_swvl2),
    max_sm = max(era5l_swvl2),
    mean_gpp = mean(GPP_NT_VUT_REF),
    correlation = cor(
      era5l_swvl2,
      GPP_NT_VUT_REF,
      method = "spearman"
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

soil_stats |>
  rename(
    "Site ID" = site_id,
    "Ecosystem" = igbp,
    "Paired days (n)" = n,
    "Years (n)" = n_years,
    "Mean SWC (m³/m³)" = mean_sm,
    "Min. SWC (m³/m³)" = min_sm,
    "Max. SWC (m³/m³)" = max_sm,
    "Mean GPP (g C/m²/day)" = mean_gpp,
    "Spearman's rho" = correlation
  ) |>
  kable(digits = 3)
```

The relationship between volumetric soil water content and summer GPP varied among the five study sites (Figure 2). The analysis comprised 4,324 paired daily observations across eight to ten years per site. Spearman's correlation coefficients ranged from −0.228 to 0.300, indicating generally weak associations between soil water content and productivity (Table 4).

The strongest positive association was observed at the cropland site CZ-KrP (ρ = 0.300), where GPP generally increased with soil water content before declining slightly at the upper end of the observed range. In contrast, JP-Api exhibited a negative association (ρ = −0.228), with a reduction in productivity at higher soil water content. The evergreen forest CA-Ca1 and grassland CH-Rtb showed relatively weak relationships (ρ = 0.080 and −0.033, respectively).

The wetland US-Elm exhibited the lowest mean summer GPP (1.17 g C m⁻² day⁻¹), with limited variation in productivity across the observed soil moisture range. Overall, no consistent soil moisture threshold could be visually identified across the five study sites, although CZ-KrP exhibited the clearest reduction in productivity under relatively dry soil conditions.

### Temperature sensitivity of productivity

**Research question:** How does the relationship between air temperature and GPP differ among the five study sites?

To investigate site-specific relationships between air temperature and ecosystem productivity, daily air temperature estimates from ERA5-Land were compared with daily gross primary productivity (GPP) derived from FLUXNET. Only days with available observations for both variables were included. Relationships were visualized separately for each study site using scatterplots and locally weighted regression curves to explore potential nonlinear responses.

```{r}
#| label: fig-temperature-productivity
#| fig-cap: "Relationship between ERA5-Land daily air temperature and FLUXNET gross primary productivity across the five study sites."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 8

temperature_gpp <- site_daily |>
  filter(
    !is.na(era5l_t2m_C),
    !is.na(GPP_NT_VUT_REF)
  )

ggplot(
  temperature_gpp,
  aes(
    x = era5l_t2m_C,
    y = GPP_NT_VUT_REF,
    color = igbp
  )
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.2, size = 0.8) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "loess",
    se = FALSE,
    linewidth = 1.2
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ site_id, ncol = 2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = eco_cols) +
  labs(
    x = "Daily air temperature (°C)",
    y = "Daily GPP (g C/m²/day)",
    color = "Ecosystem"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-temperature-gpp
#| tbl-cap: "Descriptive statistics for daily air temperature and gross primary productivity across the five study sites."

temperature_gpp_stats <- temperature_gpp |>
  group_by(site_id, igbp) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    n_years = n_distinct(year),
    mean_temp = mean(era5l_t2m_C),
    min_temp = min(era5l_t2m_C),
    max_temp = max(era5l_t2m_C),
    mean_gpp = mean(GPP_NT_VUT_REF),
    correlation = cor(
      era5l_t2m_C,
      GPP_NT_VUT_REF,
      method = "spearman"
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

temperature_gpp_stats |>
  rename(
    "Site ID" = site_id,
    "Ecosystem" = igbp,
    "Paired days (n)" = n,
    "Years (n)" = n_years,
    "Mean temperature (°C)" = mean_temp,
    "Min. temperature (°C)" = min_temp,
    "Max. temperature (°C)" = max_temp,
    "Mean GPP (g C/m²/day)" = mean_gpp,
    "Spearman's rho" = correlation
  ) |>
  kable(digits = 2)
```

The relationship between daily air temperature and GPP exhibited distinct patterns among the five study sites (Figure 3). At JP-Api, CA-Ca1 and CH-Rtb, productivity generally increased with air temperature, although the shape and magnitude of the relationships differed among sites. JP-Api exhibited a pronounced increase in productivity above approximately 5–10 °C, while CA-Ca1 showed an apparent plateau at higher temperatures.

In contrast, CZ-KrP exhibited a nonlinear, hump-shaped relationship, with productivity increasing at intermediate temperatures and declining at higher temperatures. The wetland US-Elm showed comparatively little variation in GPP across its observed temperature range. These results indicate substantial site-specific differences in the association between air temperature and ecosystem productivity.

## WorldClim: Climatic variability

### Annual deviations from climate normals

**Research question:** Which tower years were warmer or wetter than the 1970–2000 climate normals?

Annual climatic conditions at each FLUXNET study site were compared with the corresponding long-term climate normals from WorldClim 2.1 for the period 1970–2000 [@fick2017]. Temperature anomalies were calculated as the difference between annual mean air temperature and BIO1, while precipitation anomalies were calculated as the difference between annual cumulative precipitation and BIO12. Data completeness was assessed before calculating annual climate statistics to avoid biases associated with incomplete monitoring years. No additional gap-filling was performed.

Annual temperature and precipitation anomalies varied substantially among the five study sites (@fig-worldclim-annual-anomalies). The cropland site CZ-KrP exhibited a mean temperature anomaly of +1.57 °C, with all ten monitoring years exceeding the historical climate normal. Positive mean temperature anomalies were also observed at CH-Rtb (+0.67 °C) and US-Elm (+0.78 °C), where 11 of 14 and 16 of 17 monitoring years, respectively, were warmer than the corresponding WorldClim reference. In contrast, JP-Api exhibited a negative mean temperature anomaly of −0.83 °C.

Precipitation anomalies differed in both magnitude and direction among sites. Mean annual precipitation was lower than the historical reference at CA-Ca1 (−352.74 mm) and US-Elm (−179.97 mm), whereas CH-Rtb and CZ-KrP exhibited positive mean deviations of 87.51 and 23.77 mm, respectively.

Exceptionally large temperature anomalies were observed at CA-Ca1, particularly between 2007 and 2009, while JP-Api exhibited consistently large positive precipitation anomalies throughout its monitoring period. These discrepancies are apparent in both the annual time series and the summary of interannual variability (@fig-worldclim-mean-sd; @tbl-climate-anomalies). Given their magnitude, these site–variable combinations require additional data quality assessment before ecological interpretation.

```{r}
#| label: worldclim-annual-data

annual_data <- site_daily |>
  group_by(site_id, igbp, year) |>
  summarise(
    expected_days = if_else(
      leap_year(first(year)), 366, 365
    ),
    n_temp = n_distinct(date[!is.na(TA_F)]),
    n_prec = n_distinct(date[!is.na(P_F)]),
    n_gpp = n_distinct(
      date[!is.na(GPP_NT_VUT_REF)]
    ),
    annual_temp = mean(TA_F, na.rm = TRUE),
    annual_prec = sum(P_F, na.rm = TRUE),
    annual_gpp = sum(
      GPP_NT_VUT_REF, na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    temp_coverage = n_temp / expected_days,
    prec_coverage = n_prec / expected_days,
    gpp_coverage = n_gpp / expected_days,

    annual_temp = if_else(
      temp_coverage >= 0.95,
      annual_temp, NA_real_
    ),
    annual_prec = if_else(
      prec_coverage == 1,
      annual_prec, NA_real_
    ),
    annual_gpp = if_else(
      gpp_coverage == 1,
      annual_gpp, NA_real_
    )
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: worldclim-anomalies

annual_climate <- annual_data |>
  left_join(
    site_static |>
      select(site_id, BIO1, BIO12),
    by = "site_id"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    temp_anomaly = annual_temp - BIO1,
    prec_anomaly = annual_prec - BIO12
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-annual-coverage
#| tbl-cap: "Availability of annual climate and productivity statistics after applying data completeness criteria."

annual_climate |>
  group_by(site_id, igbp) |>
  summarise(
    total_years = n(),
    valid_temp = sum(!is.na(annual_temp)),
    valid_prec = sum(!is.na(annual_prec)),
    valid_gpp = sum(!is.na(annual_gpp)),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  rename(
    "Site ID" = site_id,
    "Ecosystem" = igbp,
    "Available years" = total_years,
    "Temperature" = valid_temp,
    "Precipitation" = valid_prec,
    "GPP" = valid_gpp
  ) |>
  kable()
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-worldclim-annual-anomalies
#| fig-cap: "Annual temperature (a) and precipitation (b) anomalies relative to the WorldClim 1970–2000 climate normals. Dashed horizontal lines indicate historical reference conditions. All panels share a common calendar-year axis, while vertical scales differ among sites."
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 10

climate_long <- annual_climate |>
  select(
    site_id, igbp, year,
    temp_anomaly, prec_anomaly
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(temp_anomaly, prec_anomaly),
    names_to = "variable",
    values_to = "anomaly"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    variable = factor(
      variable,
      levels = c("temp_anomaly", "prec_anomaly"),
      labels = c(
        "(a) Temperature anomaly (°C)",
        "(b) Precipitation anomaly (mm/year)"
      )
    )
  )

p_temp <- ggplot(
  annual_climate,

) +
  geom_col(na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +

    x = "Year",
    y = "Temperature anomaly (°C)",
    fill = "Ecosystem"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

p_prec <- ggplot(
  annual_climate,
  aes(year, prec_anomaly, fill = igbp)
) +
  geom_col(na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_wrap(~ site_id, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = eco_cols) +
  labs(
    x = "Year",
    y = "Precipitation anomaly (mm/year)",
    fill = "Ecosystem"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

(p_temp | p_prec) +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect") +
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = "a") &
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-worldclim-mean-sd
#| fig-cap: "Mean annual temperature (a) and precipitation (b) anomalies relative to the WorldClim 1970–2000 climate normals. Points represent site means and horizontal intervals represent ±1 interannual standard deviation."

climate_summary <- annual_climate |>
```
